arXiv:2611.05334v1 [math.OC] 03 Nov 2026

A simple adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging method for unconstrained convex optimization in pp-norm geometry

Bowen Li ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, Linköping University, Sweden (Email: bowen.a.li@liu.se, danqing.zhou@liu.se, and chuan.he@liu.se). All authors contributed equally to this work.    Danqing Zhou11footnotemark: 1    Chuan He11footnotemark: 1
Abstract

Efficient preconditioning plays an important role in large-scale first-order optimization. In this paper, we propose an adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging (A2\text{A}^{2}ODA) method for unconstrained convex optimization that adopts low-cost preconditioning based on pp-norm geometry for p∈[2,∞]p\in[2,\infty]. The method is line-search-free and employs a new stepsize selection technique based on an aggregated affine lower model. Its update structure is simple and unified across p∈[2,∞]p\in[2,\infty], with the case p>2p>2 requiring no more elaborate updates than the Euclidean case p=2p=2. Under a generalized local smoothness condition, we derive a convergence bound that separates the effects of constant and gap-dependent curvature, with the latter potentially yielding faster-decaying terms. In the special case of local smoothness, this bound recovers a nearly optimal convergence rate.

Keywords: Convex optimization; accelerated first-order methods; adaptive methods; pp-norm geometry; optimistic dual averaging; generalized local smoothness.

Mathematics Subject Classification: 90C25; 90C30; 90C06; 68Q25.

1 Introduction

In this paper, we consider the unconstrained convex optimization problem

minx∈ℝn⁡f⁡(x),\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}f(x), (1)

where f:ℝn→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} is a continuously differentiable convex function. We assume that problem (1) has at least one optimal solution. Since the seminal work on accelerated gradient methods [27], the development of fast first-order methods has remained a central focus in the study of smooth convex optimization. In practice, the performance of first-order methods is influenced by many factors, including the acceleration mechanism, the parameter selection, and the underlying geometry. The goal of this paper is to develop an accelerated first-order method in pp-norm geometry that adapts its parameters to the optimization trajectory and achieves a unified convergence bound for all p∈[2,∞]p\in[2,\infty].

In recent years, there has been fruitful research on first-order methods for smooth convex optimization [28, 1, 29]. In particular, many recent efforts have focused on parameter selection in first-order methods, which is often guided by estimates of the Lipschitz constant of the objective gradient. Instead of fixing the parameters based on a global Lipschitz constant, adapting them to local curvature typically leads to much faster practical progress. In this direction, there has recently been growing interest in first-order methods that adapt their parameters based on local curvature without requiring costly line searches. The use of local curvature to select stepsizes has a long history, as exemplified by the well-known Barzilai-Borwein (BB) stepsize [2]. However, directly applying the BB stepsize without line searches does not generally yield convergence guarantees for smooth convex problems. Recently, several studies have proposed novel stepsize schemes for line-search-free gradient methods and established provable convergence guarantees for solving problem (1); see, e.g., [24, 17, 36]. In addition, notable adaptive accelerated gradient methods, including AC-FGM [18] and AdaNAG [33], achieve optimal convergence rates for smooth convex optimization without requiring line searches.

Beyond parameter selection, the choice of geometry is another important aspect of first-order method design. For many constrained problems, replacing the Euclidean squared distance with a suitable Bregman divergence in first-order method design allows the resulting updates to reflect the intrinsic geometry of the feasible region. Well-known examples include the Kullback-Leibler divergence on the probability simplex [4] and the Itakura-Saito divergence on the positive orthant [3]. These examples can be unified under the general mirror descent framework [26, 4], whose update takes the form:

xk+1∈arg​minx∈X⁡{⟨∇f​(xk),x−xk⟩+γk​Dh​(x,xk)},x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X}\left\{\langle\nabla f(x_{k}),x-x_{k}\rangle+\gamma_{k}D_{h}(x,x_{k})\right\},

where γk>0\gamma_{k}>0, XX denotes the feasible region, and Dh​(x,y):=h⁡(x)−h⁡(y)−⟨∇h​(y),x−y⟩D_{h}(x,y):=h(x)-h(y)-\langle\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle is the Bregman divergence generated by hh. When h⁡(x)=‖x‖22/2h(x)=\|x\|_{2}^{2}/2, the update reduces to projected gradient descent. More generally, suitable choices of hh allow mirror descent to exploit non-Euclidean geometry. Under the relative smoothness condition

Df​(x,y)≤L​Dh​(x,y)∀x,y∈ΩD_{f}(x,y)\leq LD_{h}(x,y)\qquad\forall x,y\in\Omega

for some L>0L>0, convergence bounds of mirror descent methods can be established in terms of DhD_{h}, where Ω\Omega is a suitable convex set containing the iterates and relevant comparison points [4, 20]. Mirror descent and relative smoothness extend gradient descent and Lipschitz smoothness in the Euclidean norm, respectively, to non-Euclidean settings. Nonetheless, extending accelerated gradient methods to non-Euclidean mirror descent is nontrivial. There have been many recent studies on acceleration in mirror descent, including both specific accelerated variants [16, 12, 25] and lower bounds on achievable convergence rates [10]. In addition, adaptive mirror descent methods have also been developed [30].

Another line of research explores first-order methods that directly exploit norm geometry to shape search directions. In particular, replacing the squared Euclidean distance with the squared distance induced by a general norm yields the dual preconditioned gradient update [15]:

xk+1=xk−1γk​J∗​(∇f​(xk))∈arg​minx∈ℝn⁡{⟨∇f​(xk),x−xk⟩+γk2​‖x−xk‖2},\displaystyle x_{k+1}=x_{k}-\frac{1}{\gamma_{k}}J_{*}(\nabla f(x_{k}))\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\left\{\langle\nabla f(x_{k}),x-x_{k}\rangle+\frac{\gamma_{k}}{2}\|x-x_{k}\|^{2}\right\},

where γk>0\gamma_{k}>0, ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| and ∥⋅∥∗\|\cdot\|_{*} denote a general norm and its dual, respectively, and J∗(g)∈∂(∥⋅∥∗2/2)(g)J_{*}(g)\in\partial(\|\cdot\|_{*}^{2}/2)(g) for all g∈ℝng\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. For convex problems, this preconditioned method achieves an 𝒪⁡(T−1)\mathcal{O}(T^{-1}) convergence rate in the objective gap under a Lipschitz gradient condition defined using the general norm and its dual, together with a level-boundedness assumption [15], where TT denotes the number of iterations. This bound is analogous to that of classical gradient descent. Moreover, this preconditioned gradient descent has also been analyzed under a dual relative smoothness condition [23]. This condition serves as a dual counterpart to the primal relative smoothness condition used to analyze mirror descent [20]. In addition, accelerated variants of preconditioned gradient descent in general norm geometries have been developed in [7, 11]. In particular, when the primal and dual norms are the pp- and qq-norms, respectively, with 1/p+1/q=11/p+1/q=1 and 2≤p<∞2\leq p<\infty, these methods achieve an 𝒪⁡(T−(1+2/p))\mathcal{O}(T^{-(1+2/p)}) convergence rate in the objective gap, matching the lower bounds up to logarithmic factors [6]. From a technical standpoint, these methods rely on the uniform convexity of the proximal regularizer to control linearization errors in their accelerated updates [7, 11]. For the case p>2p>2, the resulting ppth-power proximal terms interact with the quadratic terms arising from Lipschitz smoothness, making parameter selection and the convergence analysis more involved than in the case p=2p=2 (see Remark 1). It is also noteworthy that pp-norm geometry has attracted significant recent interest in the design of deep learning optimizers, particularly in the endpoint case p=∞p=\infty, which leads to sign-based update directions; see, e.g., [13, 5, 9, 22, 31]. These theoretical advances and growing practical interest motivate the following natural question:

Can we design a line-search-free accelerated first-order method for smooth convex optimization that exploits pp-norm geometry for preconditioning throughout the range p∈[2,∞]p\in[2,\infty]?

This paper provides an affirmative answer to this question. Specifically, our proposed method employs an acceleration mechanism that combines optimistic dual averaging [32] in pp-norm geometry with weighted iterate averaging [14]. To adapt the regularization parameters, we aggregate past linearizations into an affine model and use this model to derive a new parameter selection rule that directly controls a Lyapunov potential. This construction differs fundamentally from the parameter selection rules used by existing line-search-free accelerated gradient methods in the case p=2p=2 [18, 33].

Moreover, our analysis relies on the relaxed dual-potential expansion inequality in Lemma 1, which avoids the need for a uniform convexity inequality for the proximal regularizer. Consequently, our method directly uses the squared pp-norm as the proximal regularizer for p>2p>2, in contrast to existing accelerated methods that rely on pp-uniformly convex regularizers [7, 11] (see Remark 1). On the theoretical side, we establish an accelerated convergence rate for the proposed method under a generalized local smoothness condition (see Assumption 1(b)). This condition incorporates gap-dependent curvature into the local smoothness condition and allows us to distinguish the contributions of the constant and gap-dependent curvature terms to the convergence bound. Our main contributions are summarized below.

  • •

    We develop an adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging (A2\text{A}^{2}ODA) method under pp-norm geometry for solving problem (1). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first line-search-free first-order method that combines adaptive acceleration with squared pp-norm regularization in a unified framework covering all p∈[2,∞]p\in[2,\infty].

  • •

    Under the generalized local smoothness condition (Assumption 1(b)), we establish a unified convergence bound for Algorithm 3.4 across all p∈[2,∞]p\in[2,\infty] that explicitly separates the contributions of constant and gap-dependent curvature (see Theorem 2). In the special case of local smoothness, this bound recovers a nearly optimal convergence rate (see Section 3.4).

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce the notation and preliminary results. In Section 3, we present the proposed algorithm and state its convergence guarantees. The proof of our main convergence result is presented in Section 4. Additional lemmas and proofs are deferred to the appendix.

2 Notation and preliminaries

Throughout this paper, we use ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+} to denote the nn-dimensional Euclidean space and the set of nonnegative real numbers, respectively, and ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle to denote the standard inner product. Let ∂h⁡(x)\partial h(x) denote the convex subdifferential of hh at xx. The Fenchel-Young equality holds if and only if u∈∂h⁡(x)u\in\partial h(x):

h⁡(x)+h∗​(u)=⟨x,u⟩.\displaystyle h(x)+h^{*}(u)=\langle x,u\rangle. (2)

For x,y∈ℝnx,y\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and gy∈∂h⁡(y)g_{y}\in\partial h(y), define the generalized Bregman divergence by Dhgy​(x,y):=h⁡(x)−h⁡(y)−⟨gy,x−y⟩D_{h}^{g_{y}}(x,y):=h(x)-h(y)-\langle g_{y},x-y\rangle. Then, for any pair of conjugate exponents p∈[2,∞]p\in[2,\infty] and q∈[1,2]q\in[1,2], one can verify that

Jq​(u)∈∂Vq​(u),‖Jq​(u)‖p=‖u‖q,⟨Jq​(u),u⟩=‖u‖q2.\displaystyle J_{q}(u)\in\partial V_{q}(u),\qquad\|J_{q}(u)\|_{p}=\|u\|_{q},\qquad\langle J_{q}(u),u\rangle=\|u\|_{q}^{2}. (5)

V2​(u+v)=V2​(u)+⟨J2​(u),v⟩+V2​(v).\displaystyle V_{2}(u+v)=V_{2}(u)+\langle J_{2}(u),v\rangle+V_{2}(v). (7)
Lemma 1 (Relaxed dual-potential expansion).

Let q∈[1,2)q\in[1,2), and let VqV_{q} and JqJ_{q} be defined in (3) and (4), respectively. Then,

c​Vq​(u+v)≤Vq​(u)+⟨Jq​(u),v⟩+(1+22/rq​c(1−crq)1/rq)​Vq​(v)\displaystyle c\,V_{q}(u+v)\leq V_{q}(u)+\langle J_{q}(u),v\rangle+\bigg(1+\frac{2^{2/r_{q}}c}{(1-c^{r_{q}})^{1/{r_{q}}}}\bigg)\,V_{q}(v) (8)

holds for all u,v∈ℝn,c∈(0,1)u,v\in\mathbb{R}^{n},c\in(0,1), where rqr_{q} is defined in (6).

Remark 1.

Existing accelerated methods in pp-norm geometry typically rely on pp-uniformly convex proximal regularizers for p>2p>2 [7, 11]. The resulting ppth-power proximal terms cannot be directly balanced against the quadratic errors arising from Lipschitz smoothness, requiring additional approximation arguments and more involved parameter choices.

In contrast, our method directly uses the squared pp-norm as the proximal regularizer, without requiring a uniform convexity lower bound. The key technical ingredient in our analysis is the relaxed dual-potential expansion in Lemma 1, which controls perturbations through a quadratic term in the dual norm. Combined with our adaptive parameter-selection rule, this inequality provides an alternative approach to acceleration in pp-norm geometry and simplifies the convergence analysis.

We make the following assumptions throughout the paper.

Assumption 1.
  1. (a)

    The function ff is convex and attains its minimum, with optimal value denoted by f∗:=minx∈ℝn⁡f⁡(x)f_{*}:=\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}f(x).

  2. (b)

    Let p∈[2,∞]p\in[2,\infty] and q∈[1,2]q\in[1,2] be conjugate exponents with 1/p+1/q=11/p+1/q=1, and let ν∈[0,1)\nu\in[0,1). For every compact convex set Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, there exist constants Lp​(Ω),Hp​(Ω)≥0L_{p}(\Omega),H_{p}(\Omega)\geq 0 such that

    ‖∇f​(x)−∇f​(y)‖q2≤2​(Lp​(Ω)+Hp​(Ω)​max⁡{Δ⁡(x),Δ⁡(y)}ν)​Df​(x,y)\displaystyle\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_{q}^{2}\leq 2\left(L_{p}(\Omega)+H_{p}(\Omega)\max\{\Delta(x),\Delta(y)\}^{\nu}\right)D_{f}(x,y) (9)

    holds for all x,y∈Ωx,y\in\Omega, where Δ⁡(x):=f⁡(x)−f∗\Delta(x):=f(x)-f_{*}.

Remark 2.

Assumption 1(b) is a cocoercivity-type generalized local smoothness condition. This condition is related to local smoothness [21] and gap-dependent generalized smoothness [19]. Applying (9) to both (x,y)(x,y) and (y,x)(y,x), and then using Hölder’s inequality, yields the following Lipschitz-type generalized local smoothness condition:

‖∇f​(x)−∇f​(y)‖q≤(Lp​(Ω)+Hp​(Ω)​max⁡{Δ⁡(x),Δ⁡(y)}ν)​‖x−y‖p∀x,y∈Ω.\displaystyle\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_{q}\leq(L_{p}(\Omega)+H_{p}(\Omega)\max\{\Delta(x),\Delta(y)\}^{\nu})\|x-y\|_{p}\qquad\forall x,y\in\Omega. (10)

Conversely, for any given Ω\Omega containing x∗x_{*}, (9) holds with constants Lp​(Ω),Hp​(Ω)≥0L_{p}(\Omega),H_{p}(\Omega)\geq 0 provided that

‖∇f​(x)−∇f​(y)‖q≤(Lp​(Ω)+2−ν​Hp​(Ω)​max⁡{Δ⁡(x),Δ⁡(y)}ν)​‖x−y‖p∀x,y∈Ω¯,\displaystyle\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_{q}\leq(L_{p}(\Omega)+2^{-\nu}H_{p}(\Omega)\max\{\Delta(x),\Delta(y)\}^{\nu})\|x-y\|_{p}\qquad\forall x,y\in\bar{\Omega},

where Ω¯\bar{\Omega} is a suitably enlarged compact convex set containing Ω\Omega. A precise choice of Ω¯\bar{\Omega} and a proof of this implication are provided in Appendix B. Thus, the cocoercivity-type and Lipschitz-type generalized local smoothness conditions are equivalent, up to an enlargement of the domain and a change in constants.

When ν=0\nu=0, Assumption 1(b) reduces to the usual local smoothness condition. For ν>0\nu>0, it separates the curvature bound into a constant part Lp​(Ω)L_{p}(\Omega) and a gap-dependent part Hp​(Ω)​max⁡{Δ⁡(x),Δ⁡(y)}νH_{p}(\Omega)\max\{\Delta(x),\Delta(y)\}^{\nu}, which vanishes as the objective values approach the minimum. This decomposition allows the leading term of the convergence bound to depend on Lp​(Ω)L_{p}(\Omega), which can be substantially smaller than a uniform curvature bound over Ω\Omega, while the gap-dependent curvature contributes terms that may decay faster.

3 An adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging method

In this section, we propose an adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging (A2\text{A}^{2}ODA) method in pp-norm geometry for p∈[2,∞]p\in[2,\infty] and establish its convergence properties under the generalized local smoothness condition stated in Assumption 1(b). Specifically, we first describe the main components of the method in Sections 3.1-3.3 and then present the complete algorithm and its convergence results in Section 3.4.

Before proceeding, we let {λk}\{\lambda_{k}\} be the positive weights for averaging iterates and gradients, and define the cumulative weights by Ak=∑i=1kλiA_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i} for all k≥1k\geq 1. The A2\text{A}^{2}ODA method generates two sequences: the optimistic dual-averaging iterates {yk}\{y_{k}\} and the weighted-average iterates {xk}\{x_{k}\}. For convenience, we denote the sequences of function values and gradients evaluated at {xk}\{x_{k}\} by {fk}\{f_{k}\} and {gk}\{g_{k}\}, respectively, where fk=f⁡(xk)f_{k}=f(x_{k}) and gk=∇f​(xk)g_{k}=\nabla f(x_{k}) for all k≥1k\geq 1.

3.1 Optimistic dual averaging and acceleration

The proposed method combines optimistic dual averaging with weighted primal averaging to achieve acceleration. It mainly consists of three parts: dual averaging to accumulate past gradients, optimism to predict the next gradient contribution, and weighted primal averaging to construct the iterates at which gradients are evaluated.

Following the dual-averaging strategy [35], we maintain the weighted gradient sum

s0=0,sk=∑i=1kλi​gi,∀k≥1.s_{0}=0,\qquad s_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}g_{i},\qquad\forall k\geq 1.

At the beginning of iteration kk, the new gradient gkg_{k} is not yet available. We therefore use the most recent gradient gk−1g_{k-1} to predict the contribution of gkg_{k} to sks_{k}, forming

s~k=sk−1+λk​gk−1∀k≥1.\tilde{s}_{k}=s_{k-1}+\lambda_{k}g_{k-1}\qquad\forall k\geq 1.

The term λk​gk−1\lambda_{k}g_{k-1} constitutes the optimistic part: it adds a prediction of the next weighted gradient before that gradient is observed, as in optimistic follow-the-regularized-leader methods [32].

The optimistic dual-averaging iterate yky_{k} is then obtained by minimizing the sum of the predicted linear model and a regularization term:

yk∈arg​miny∈ℝn⁡{⟨s~k,y−x0⟩+γk2​‖y−x0‖p2},y_{k}\in\argmin_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\left\{\langle\tilde{s}_{k},y-x_{0}\rangle+\frac{\gamma_{k}}{2}\|y-x_{0}\|_{p}^{2}\right\},

where γk>0\gamma_{k}>0 controls the regularization strength. Our novel adaptive strategy for updating γk\gamma_{k} will be introduced later.

To achieve acceleration, a key ingredient is the coupling of optimistic updates with gradient evaluations at running weighted averages [14]. Specifically, we form the weighted primal average

xk=Ak−1Ak​xk−1+λkAk​yk=1Ak​∑i=1kλi​yi,x_{k}=\frac{A_{k-1}}{A_{k}}x_{k-1}+\frac{\lambda_{k}}{A_{k}}y_{k}=\frac{1}{A_{k}}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}y_{i},

and evaluate the new gradient at the averaged iterate xkx_{k}, rather than at yky_{k}, setting gk=∇f​(xk)g_{k}=\nabla f(x_{k}).

3.2 Aggregated affine lower model for adaptive regularization

We now motivate our adaptive strategy for updating the regularization parameters based on an accumulated affine lower model. Following the estimate-sequence and approximate-duality-gap techniques [34, 8], we aggregate supporting affine functions and add a regularization term.

For any x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, we define the aggregated affine lower model φk\varphi_{k} by

φk​(x):=ck+⟨sk,x−x0⟩=∑i=1kλi​(fi+⟨gi,x−xi⟩)≤Ak​f​(x)\displaystyle\varphi_{k}(x):=c_{k}+\langle s_{k},x-x_{0}\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}(f_{i}+\langle g_{i},x-x_{i}\rangle)\leq A_{k}f(x) (11)
withck:=∑i=1kλi​(fi+⟨gi,x0−xi⟩),\displaystyle\text{with}\quad c_{k}:=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}(f_{i}+\langle g_{i},x_{0}-x_{i}\rangle),

where the inequality is due to the convexity of ff. This model collects the first-order information obtained along the optimization trajectory. It requires only the vector sks_{k} and the scalar ckc_{k}, both of which can be updated recursively.

Directly minimizing φk\varphi_{k} over ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} does not generally yield a useful comparison value. We therefore define the regularized estimating function for any γ>0\gamma>0 and its minimum value by

ψk​(x,γ):=φk​(x)+γ2​‖x−x0‖p2,mk​(γ):=minx∈ℝn⁡ψk​(x,γ)=ck−‖sk‖q22​γ,\displaystyle\psi_{k}(x;\gamma):=\varphi_{k}(x)+\frac{\gamma}{2}\|x-x_{0}\|_{p}^{2},\qquad m_{k}(\gamma):=\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\psi_{k}(x;\gamma)=c_{k}-\frac{\|s_{k}\|_{q}^{2}}{2\gamma}, (12)

where the last equality follows from Fenchel conjugacy. For any minimizer x∗x_{*} of ff, (11) then implies

mk​(γ)≤ψk​(x∗,γ)≤Ak​f∗+γ2​‖x∗−x0‖p2.\displaystyle m_{k}(\gamma)\leq\psi_{k}(x_{*};\gamma)\leq A_{k}f_{*}+\frac{\gamma}{2}\|x_{*}-x_{0}\|_{p}^{2}. (13)

Although mk​(γ)m_{k}(\gamma) is not necessarily a lower bound on Ak​f∗A_{k}f_{*}, this inequality provides the comparison needed to control the objective gap.

Motivated by (13), we seek a regularization parameter satisfying

Ak​fk≤mk​(γ)+ρk2​γ,\displaystyle A_{k}f_{k}\leq m_{k}(\gamma)+\rho_{k}^{2}\gamma, (14)

where ρk>0\rho_{k}>0 is a scale to be specified later. The additional term ρk2​γ\rho_{k}^{2}\gamma is chosen to scale linearly with γ\gamma, matching the regularization term in (13). The condition (14) is computable without knowing f∗f_{*}. Combining it with (13) yields

fk−f∗≤γAk​(ρk2+12​‖x∗−x0‖p2).\displaystyle f_{k}-f_{*}\leq\frac{\gamma}{A_{k}}\Big(\rho_{k}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\|x_{*}-x_{0}\|_{p}^{2}\Big). (15)

For a fixed ρk\rho_{k}, the resulting bound is proportional to γ\gamma.

Given γk>0\gamma_{k}>0 and a safeguard parameter θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1), we select the smallest γ≥θ​γk\gamma\geq\theta\gamma_{k} satisfying (14):

γk+1:=min⁡{γ≥θ​γk:Ak​fk≤mk​(γ)+ρk2​γ}.\displaystyle\gamma_{k+1}:=\min\left\{\gamma\geq\theta\gamma_{k}:A_{k}f_{k}\leq m_{k}(\gamma)+\rho_{k}^{2}\gamma\right\}. (16)

The safeguard limits the decrease in the regularization parameter, while the estimating-function comparison (14) determines whether a value larger than θ​γk\theta\gamma_{k} is needed. Denote χk:=Ak​fk−ck\chi_{k}:=A_{k}f_{k}-c_{k}. Using the expression for mk​(γ)m_{k}(\gamma) in (12), we can rewrite the update (16) explicitly as

γk+1=max⁡{θ​γk,χk+χk2+2​ρk2​‖sk‖q22​ρk2}.\gamma_{k+1}=\max\left\{\theta\gamma_{k},\,\frac{\chi_{k}+\sqrt{\chi_{k}^{2}+2\rho_{k}^{2}\|s_{k}\|_{q}^{2}}}{2\rho_{k}^{2}}\right\}.

Since (14) holds with γ=γk+1\gamma=\gamma_{k+1}, it follows from (15) that

fk−f∗≤γk+1Ak​(ρk2+12​‖x∗−x0‖p2).f_{k}-f_{*}\leq\frac{\gamma_{k+1}}{A_{k}}\Bigl(\rho_{k}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\|x_{*}-x_{0}\|_{p}^{2}\Bigr).

3.3 Bounded Lyapunov-potential certificate

We now use the estimating-function comparison in Section 3.2 to construct a natural potential sequence {𝒫k}\{\mathcal{P}_{k}\} for the convergence analysis. Specifically, for all k≥1k\geq 1, define

𝒫k:=Ak​fk−mk​(γk+1)=χk+‖sk‖q22​γk+1,\mathcal{P}_{k}:=A_{k}f_{k}-m_{k}(\gamma_{k+1})=\chi_{k}+\frac{\|s_{k}\|_{q}^{2}}{2\gamma_{k+1}},

where the last equality follows from the definition of χk\chi_{k} and (12). The connection between this potential and the objective gap follows from (13), which gives

𝒫k≥Ak​(fk−f∗)−γk+12​‖x∗−x0‖p2.\mathcal{P}_{k}\geq A_{k}(f_{k}-f_{*})-\frac{\gamma_{k+1}}{2}\|x_{*}-x_{0}\|_{p}^{2}.

Thus, controlling 𝒫k\mathcal{P}_{k} relative to γk+1\gamma_{k+1} provides a bound on the objective gap. In addition, the condition (14), with γ=γk+1\gamma=\gamma_{k+1}, ensures that

𝒫k=χk+‖sk‖q22​γk+1≤ρk2​γk+1.\mathcal{P}_{k}=\chi_{k}+\frac{\|s_{k}\|_{q}^{2}}{2\gamma_{k+1}}\leq\rho_{k}^{2}\gamma_{k+1}.

This bounded potential condition also provides a basis for establishing the boundedness of the iterates {xk}\{x_{k}\} and {yk}\{y_{k}\}. A detailed statement will be given in Theorem 1.

3.4 The A2\text{A}^{2}ODA method and its convergence rate

We now summarize the A2\text{A}^{2}ODA method in Algorithm 3.4, which combines the updates described above.

 

Algorithm 1 A2\text{A}^{2}ODA: An Adaptive Accelerated Optimistic Dual Averaging method

 
Input:Initialiteratex 0 ∈R n satisfying∇f(x 0 )≠0,aconjugatepair(p,q)withq∈[1,2]and1/p+1/q=1,averagingscalem≥2,initialregularizationparameterγ 1 >0,andscalingparametersα,θsatisfyingθ∈(0,1)andα​>​2(1+e+e/θ).
Setf 0 =f(x 0 ),g 0 =∇f(x 0 ),s 0 =0,c 0 =0,A 0 =0,andρ 0 =0.
for k=1,2,… do
Computetheaveragingweights: λ k = ( 1 + k - 1 m - 1 ) m - 1 , A k = A k - 1 + λ k .
Performanoptimisticdualaveragingstep: ~ s k = s k - 1 + λ k g k - 1 , y k = x 0 + 1 γ k J q ( - ~ s k ) , x k = A k - 1 A k x k - 1 + λ k A k y k .

ρk=max⁡{ρk−1,‖yk−x0‖pα}.\rho_{k}=\max\bigg\{\rho_{k-1},\frac{\|y_{k}-x_{0}\|_{p}}{\alpha}\bigg\}. (17)
Updatetheaccumulatedgradientandaffinemodel: s k = s k - 1 + λ k g k , c k = c k - 1 + λ k ( f k + ⟨ g k , x 0 - x k ⟩ ) , χ k = A k f k - c k .

end for
 

WenowmakeafewremarksaboutAlgorithm3.4.

  • •

    The parameter m≥2m\geq 2 controls the growth of the averaging weights: for fixed mm, λk=Θ⁡(km−1)\lambda_{k}=\Theta(k^{m-1}) and Ak=Θ⁡(km)A_{k}=\Theta(k^{m}). In particular, m=2m=2 gives λk=k\lambda_{k}=k and Ak=k⁡(k+1)/2A_{k}=k(k+1)/2, recovering the linearly increasing weights used in accelerated optimistic dual averaging [14]. Allowing m>2m>2 provides flexibility to exploit the diminishing gap-dependent curvature under generalized local smoothness, potentially yielding faster decay of the corresponding terms in the convergence bound.

    The benefit of increasing mm depends on its interaction with the adaptive regularization. Indeed, when the sequence of radius scales {ρk}\{\rho_{k}\} is bounded, the objective-gap bound derived above is governed by γk+1/Ak\gamma_{k+1}/A_{k}. Thus, faster growth of AkA_{k} can translate into faster convergence only if it is not offset by the growth of γk+1\gamma_{k+1}. The convergence analysis below quantifies this interaction.

  • •

    The scale ρk\rho_{k} controls the tolerance in the estimating-function comparison (see (14)) and therefore affects the update of the regularization parameter γk+1\gamma_{k+1}. We choose

    ρk=1α​max1≤i≤k​{‖yi−x0‖p}\rho_{k}=\frac{1}{\alpha}\max_{1\leq i\leq k}\{\|y_{i}-x_{0}\|_{p}\}

    so that this scale adapts to the observed size of the optimization trajectory, without requiring prior knowledge of the distance from x0x_{0} to a minimizer.

    This choice balances two effects: a larger ρk\rho_{k} relaxes the estimating-function comparison and may allow a smaller regularization parameter, but it also increases the radius-dependent term in the objective-gap bound. This adaptive update is designed to achieve a favorable dependence on problem constants while using only quantities already available from the iterates. A simpler alternative is to use a fixed scale ρk≡ρ>0\rho_{k}\equiv\rho>0.

  • •

    The initial regularization parameter γ1\gamma_{1} can be selected through an optional backtracking line search, similar to that in [18]. We present its procedure as follows:

    This procedure terminates after finitely many trials: differentiability of ff at x0x_{0} ensures acceptance for all sufficiently large γ\gamma, while f≥f∗f\geq f_{*} and g0≠0g_{0}\neq 0 ensure rejection for all sufficiently small γ\gamma. Let LpL_{p} and HpH_{p} be the corresponding curvature moduli on a compact convex set 𝒮p\mathcal{S}_{p} containing the iterates and a minimizer x∗x_{*}, where 𝒮p\mathcal{S}_{p} will be specified in Theorem 1 below. Under Assumption 1, the calibrated parameter γ1\gamma_{1} satisfies

    ‖g0‖q22​Δ​(x0)≤γ1<2​(Lp+Hp​Δ​(x0)ν).\frac{\|g_{0}\|_{q}^{2}}{2\Delta(x_{0})}\leq\gamma_{1}<2\bigl(L_{p}+H_{p}\Delta(x_{0})^{\nu}\bigr). (18)

    A proof of this bound is provided in Appendix C. The calibration requires no prior knowledge of the smoothness constants and improves the dependence of the convergence rate on LpL_{p} and HpH_{p}, as detailed in Remark 5. Since the line search is performed only during initialization, subsequent iterations remain line-search-free.

𝒫0=0,𝒫k:=χk+1γk+1​Vq​(−sk)∀k≥1,\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{0}=0,\qquad\mathcal{P}_{k}:=\chi_{k}+\frac{1}{\gamma_{k+1}}V_{q}(-s_{k})\qquad\forall k\geq 1, (20)

The following theorem establishes upper bounds on {𝒫k}\{\mathcal{P}_{k}\} and the boundedness of the iterates generated by Algorithm 3.4.

Theorem 1.

Suppose that Assumption 1(a) holds. Let {(xk,yk,γk,ρk)}\{(x_{k},y_{k},\gamma_{k},\rho_{k})\} be generated by Algorithm 3.4 and let {𝒫k}\{\mathcal{P}_{k}\} be defined in (20). Fix any minimizer x∗x_{*} of ff, and denote

Cθ=2​(1+e+e/θ),andρ¯=max⁡{‖g0‖q/(α​γ1),Cθ​‖x0−x∗‖p/α2−Cθ2}.C_{\theta}=2(1+e+e/\theta),\quad\text{and}\quad\bar{\rho}=\max\Big\{\|g_{0}\|_{q}/(\alpha\gamma_{1}),\,C_{\theta}\|x_{0}-x_{*}\|_{p}/\sqrt{\alpha^{2}-C_{\theta}^{2}}\Big\}. (21)

Then, 0<ρk≤ρ¯0<\rho_{k}\leq\bar{\rho} for k≥1k\geq 1, and for any k≥0k\geq 0,

𝒫k≤ρk2​γk+1.\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{k}\leq{\rho_{k}^{2}}\gamma_{k+1}. (22)

xk,yk,x∗∈𝒮p:={x∈ℝn:‖x−x0‖p≤α​ρ¯}.\displaystyle x_{k},y_{k},x_{*}\in\mathcal{S}_{p}:=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\|x-x_{0}\|_{p}\leq\alpha\bar{\rho}\right\}. (23)

hold for any k≥1k\geq 1. Using these identities, we obtain

≤ρk2​γk+⟨zk,sk−s~k⟩≤ρk2​γk+‖zk‖p​‖sk−s~k‖q​≤(43)(44)(45)​ρk2​hk​Mkaq+4​hk​Mk​α2​ρk2,\displaystyle\leq{\rho_{k}}^{2}\gamma_{k}+\langle z_{k},s_{k}-\tilde{s}_{k}\rangle\leq{\rho_{k}}^{2}\gamma_{k}+\|z_{k}\|_{p}\|s_{k}-\tilde{s}_{k}\|_{q}\overset{\eqref{ineq:upbd-gammak-caseB}\eqref{ineq:sk-tsk-B}\eqref{ineq:zk-tsk-B}}{\leq}\frac{{\rho_{k}}^{2}h_{k}M_{k}}{a_{q}}+4h_{k}M_{k}\alpha^{2}\rho_{k}^{2},

The next lemma provides upper bounds for {γk}k≥2\{\gamma_{k}\}_{k\geq 2} generated by Algorithm 3.4.

Lemma 6.

Suppose that Assumption 1 holds. Let {γk}\{\gamma_{k}\} be generated by Algorithm 3.4, and let rqr_{q}, {ℓk}\{\ell_{k}\},{Mk}\{M_{k}\}, Γℬ\Gamma_{\mathcal{B}}, and Γ0\Gamma_{0} be defined in (6), (30), (31), (42), and (46) respectively. and ​rm,ν,q​(T)\displaystyle\text{and }\;r_{m,\nu,q}(T) ={T−m,m<3−2/q1−ν,T−3−2/q1−ν​(log⁡T)2/q−11−ν,m=3−2/q1−ν,T−3−2/q1−ν,m>3−2/q1−ν.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}T^{-m},&m<\frac{3-2/q}{1-\nu},\\ T^{-\frac{3-2/q}{1-\nu}}(\log T)^{\frac{2/q-1}{1-\nu}},&m=\frac{3-2/q}{1-\nu},\\ T^{-\frac{3-2/q}{1-\nu}},&m>\frac{3-2/q}{1-\nu}.\end{cases}

Suppose that f:ℝn→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} is convex and continuously differentiable and attains its minimum value f∗f_{*}. implies the cocoercivity-type condition

Appendix C Proof of the calibration bound

Since γ1\gamma_{1} is accepted and f⁡(x1)≥f∗f(x_{1})\geq f_{*}, the sufficient-decrease condition gives ‖g0‖q22​γ1≤Δ⁡(x0)\frac{\|g_{0}\|_{q}^{2}}{2\gamma_{1}}\leq\Delta(x_{0}), which proves the lower bound.

For the upper bound, we first show that the rejected trial x1​(γ1/2)x_{1}(\gamma_{1}/2) belongs to 𝒮p\mathcal{S}_{p} defined in (23). Lemma 8.

Let cA=(m​(m−1)m−1)−1c_{A}=(m(m-1)^{m-1})^{-1}, and Ch=2m−1/cAC_{h}=2^{m-1}/c_{A}. For m≥2m\geq 2 and k≥2k\geq 2, the weights λk\lambda_{k} and AkA_{k} in Algorithm 3.4 satisfy

1≤λkλk−1≤e,cA​km≤Ak≤km,km−22​(m−1)2​m−2≤hk:=λk22​Ak−1≤Ch​km−2.\displaystyle 1\leq\frac{\lambda_{k}}{\lambda_{k-1}}\leq e,\qquad c_{A}k^{m}\leq A_{k}\leq k^{m},\qquad\frac{k^{m-2}}{2(m-1)^{2m-2}}\leq h_{k}:=\frac{\lambda_{k}^{2}}{2A_{k-1}}\leq C_{h}k^{m-2}. (73)
Proof.

We prove the results given in (73) one by one. First, for k≥2k\geq 2, using the update of λk\lambda_{k} in (4), the first inequality can be verified directly by

1≤λkλk−1=(k+m−2k+m−3)m−1≤(1+1m−1)m−1≤e.\displaystyle 1\leq\frac{\lambda_{k}}{\lambda_{k-1}}=\left(\frac{k+m-2}{k+m-3}\right)^{m-1}\leq\left(1+\frac{1}{m-1}\right)^{m-1}\leq e.

Second, for every k≥1k\geq 1, we have km−1≤1+k−1m−1=λk1/(m−1)≤k.\frac{k}{m-1}\leq 1+\frac{k-1}{m-1}=\lambda_{k}^{1/(m-1)}\leq k. Hence, taking the m−1m-1 power, summing λi\lambda_{i} from i=1i=1 to kk, and using the update form of AkA_{k} in (4), we obtain

km−1(m−1)m−1≤λk≤km−1,1(m−1)m−1​∑i=1kim−1≤Ak≤∑i=1kim−1.\displaystyle\frac{k^{m-1}}{(m-1)^{m-1}}\leq\lambda_{k}\leq k^{m-1},\qquad\frac{1}{(m-1)^{m-1}}\sum_{i=1}^{k}i^{m-1}\leq A_{k}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{k}i^{m-1}.

Using the elementary inequality km/m≤∑i=1kim−1≤kmk^{m}/m\leq\sum_{i=1}^{k}i^{m-1}\leq k^{m} for m≥1m\geq 1, we directly have cA​km≤Ak≤kmc_{A}k^{m}\leq A_{k}\leq k^{m} by using the definition cA=(m​(m−1)m−1)−1c_{A}=(m(m-1)^{m-1})^{-1}. Finally, for k≥2k\geq 2, the inequality k−1≥k/2k-1\geq k/2 gives

hk=λk22​Ak−1≤k2​m−22​cA​(k−1)m≤2m−1cA​km−2=Ch​km−2.\displaystyle h_{k}=\frac{\lambda_{k}^{2}}{2A_{k-1}}\leq\frac{k^{2m-2}}{2c_{A}(k-1)^{m}}\leq\frac{2^{m-1}}{c_{A}}k^{m-2}=C_{h}k^{m-2}.

For the reverse order estimate, using λk≥(k/(m−1))m−1\lambda_{k}\geq(k/(m-1))^{m-1} and Ak−1≤(k−1)mA_{k-1}\leq(k-1)^{m}, we obtain

hk=λk22​Ak−1≥k2​m−22​(m−1)2​m−2​(k−1)m≥km−22​(m−1)2​m−2.\displaystyle h_{k}=\frac{\lambda_{k}^{2}}{2A_{k-1}}\geq\frac{k^{2m-2}}{2(m-1)^{2m-2}(k-1)^{m}}\geq\frac{k^{m-2}}{2(m-1)^{2m-2}}.

This completes the proof. ∎

Lemma 9.

Let q∈[1,2)q\in[1,2), and define ωq​(t):=sgn0⁡(t)​|t|q−1\omega_{q}(t):=\operatorname{sgn}_{0}(t)|t|^{q-1} for all t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}. Then,

‖u+v‖qq≤‖u‖qq+q​∑i=1nωq​(ui)​vi+22−q​‖v‖qq\displaystyle\|u+v\|_{q}^{q}\leq\|u\|_{q}^{q}+q\sum_{i=1}^{n}\omega_{q}(u_{i})v_{i}+2^{2-q}\|v\|_{q}^{q} (74)

holds for all u,v∈ℝnu,v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.

Proof.

Define ωq​(t):=sgn0⁡(t)​|t|q−1\omega_{q}(t):=\operatorname{sgn}_{0}(t)|t|^{q-1} for all t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}. We first show that, for all q∈[1,2)q\in[1,2),

|ωq​(a)−ωq​(b)|≤22−q​|a−b|q−1∀a,b∈ℝ.\displaystyle|\omega_{q}(a)-\omega_{q}(b)|\leq 2^{2-q}|a-b|^{q-1}\qquad\forall a,b\in\mathbb{R}. (75)

To prove the claim, we consider the following three cases.

  • (i)

    If a​b>0ab>0, the subadditivity of t↦tq−1t\mapsto t^{q-1} on ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+} gives |ωq​(a)−ωq​(b)|=||a|q−1−|b|q−1|≤||a|−|b||q−1=|a−b|q−1|\omega_{q}(a)-\omega_{q}(b)|=\big||a|^{q-1}-|b|^{q-1}\big|\leq\big||a|-|b|\big|^{q-1}=|a-b|^{q-1}, which further implies (75) using q∈[1,2)q\in[1,2);

  • (ii)

    If a​b<0ab<0, the concavity of t↦tq−1t\mapsto t^{q-1} on ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+} gives |ωq​(a)−ωq​(b)|=|a|q−1+|b|q−1≤22−q​(|a|+|b|)q−1=22−q​|a−b|q−1|\omega_{q}(a)-\omega_{q}(b)|=|a|^{q-1}+|b|^{q-1}\leq 2^{2-q}(|a|+|b|)^{q-1}=2^{2-q}|a-b|^{q-1};

  • (iii)

    If a​b=0ab=0, then |ωq​(a)−ωq​(b)|≤|a−b|q−1|\omega_{q}(a)-\omega_{q}(b)|\leq|a-b|^{q-1}, which further implies (75).

Combining all these cases establishes (75). Moreover, for any q∈[1,2)q\in[1,2), the function t↦|t|qt\mapsto|t|^{q} is locally absolutely continuous, and its derivative equals q​ωq​(t)q\omega_{q}(t) almost everywhere. Thus, for all a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R},

|a+b|q−|a|q−q​ωq​(a)​b\displaystyle|a+b|^{q}-|a|^{q}-q\omega_{q}(a)b =q​∫01(ωq​(a+t​b)−ωq​(a))​b​𝑑t≤q​∫01|ωq​(a+t​b)−ωq​(a)|​|b|​𝑑t\displaystyle=q\int_{0}^{1}(\omega_{q}(a+tb)-\omega_{q}(a))b\,\mathrm{d}t\leq q\int_{0}^{1}|\omega_{q}(a+tb)-\omega_{q}(a)|\,|b|\,\mathrm{d}t
≤(75)​q​ 22−q​|b|q​∫01tq−1​𝑑t=22−q​|b|q.\displaystyle\overset{\eqref{ineq:diff-jq}}{\leq}q\,2^{2-q}|b|^{q}\int_{0}^{1}t^{q-1}\,\mathrm{d}t=2^{2-q}|b|^{q}.

Applying it with a=uia=u_{i} and b=vib=v_{i} and summing over i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n yields the desired result (74). ∎

Lemma 10.

Let a,b,c≥0a,b,c\geq 0, ν∈[0,1)\nu\in[0,1). If a≤b+c​aν,a\leq b+ca^{\nu}, then a≤2​b+(2​c)11−ν.a\leq 2b+(2c)^{\frac{1}{1-\nu}}.

Proof.

By the weighted Young’s inequality, we have

c​aν=12​[(2​c)1/(1−ν)]1−ν​aν≤12​((1−ν)​(2​c)11−ν+ν​a)≤12​((2​c)11−ν+a).\displaystyle ca^{\nu}=\frac{1}{2}\bigl[(2c)^{1/(1-\nu)}\bigr]^{1-\nu}a^{\nu}\leq\frac{1}{2}\Big((1-\nu)(2c)^{\frac{1}{1-\nu}}+\nu a\Big)\leq\frac{1}{2}\Big((2c)^{\frac{1}{1-\nu}}+a\Big).

Substituting this into the inequality a≤b+c​aνa\leq b+ca^{\nu} and rearranging gives the claim. ∎
